query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled minor amount of titanium into an AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a coherent, lubricious Ti-rich oxide surface layer during service, thereby reducing both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate across a wide temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy without additional reactive alloying elements that normally forms standard oxide scales under high temperature without significant lubricity.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small, controlled addition of titanium (e.g., around 0.5 at.%) into the alloy formulation during processing.
generation.conditions: Tested under ambient atmospheric conditions with sliding wear tests conducted over a broad temperature range (from room temperature up to approximately 900 °C) to simulate self-lubricating moving component service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The Ti addition segregates to the surface under operating conditions and oxidizes to form a coherent, nanostructured Ti-rich oxide film (likely TiO2) that acts as a protective, low-shear interface.
generation.mechanism: The lubricious oxide film reduces adhesive interactions at the sliding interface, thereby lowering friction and mitigating wear. Its formation is enabled by the high reactivity of Ti under ambient to high-temperature oxidizing conditions, which creates a self-healing, continuous layer that remains effective over a wide temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the Ti-doped HEA is expected to exhibit a significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction (potentially by around a factor of two) and the wear rate (potentially by an order of magnitude), with these improvements maintained from room temperature to high operating temperatures.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (COF and wear rate) of the standard AlCoCrFeNi HEA without Ti addition under identical wear test conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are hypothesized to hold in oxidizing environments over the specified temperature range; however, effectiveness might be limited if the environmental conditions inhibit the formation or stability of the Ti-rich oxide layer or if excessive Ti leads to undesirable phase changes in the alloy.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide layer formation, its uniformity, long-term stability, and precise quantitative improvements in friction and wear reduction are uncertain and require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one standard AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy and one alloy with an added 0.5 at.% Ti. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests over a range of temperatures (e.g., room temperature, intermediate temperatures, and near 900 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere. Characterize their surface chemistry (using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy) to verify the formation of a Ti-rich oxide layer in the modified alloy.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) during sliding tests
Wear rate quantified via wear track profiling
Surface oxide layer composition and morphology via XPS and SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped alloy does not consistently show a statistically significant decrease in both COF and wear rate compared to the standard alloy across the entire temperature range, or if no continuous Ti-rich lubricious oxide film is detected on the worn surface, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening. Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
